i have to add some scientist perspective. NOT TO COUNTER ANYTHING ALREADY SAID, BUT... working with viruses is difficult. To do the research, you need a lot of virus particles. to make lots of virus particles, you need cells that are susceptible to infection and you're usually working with live virus or sometimes a "defanged" virus. frequently, removing the payload of a virus breaks it, because either the DNA/RNA center doesn't fold right, or it doesn't bind with the internal proteins, or you've somehow made it so the virus won't replicate or assemble properly. in some cases, you can take the important proteins from the virus and drop them into another virus that you can control better, like an HIV virus without a payload. the HIV psudovirus does the infection of the cell culture and the relocation of the target (CoV) virus proteins is taken care of by the HIV machinery. in this way, you can work with a virus that may be missing a critical piece that would make it "live."

the important thing to do is go to the materials and methods of the paper and try to determine the HIV psudovirus kit they used. this shows they were using some kind of HIV system to study CoV, but may not be the smoking gun we're looking for. it could be in a subsequent publication.
